newsitem.title: USA: Democrats to fight to expand campaign funds probe.
newsitem.headline: Democrats to fight to expand campaign funds probe.

text.p: Senate Democrats said Friday they will fight to broaden an investigation into 1996 election campaign fund raising to include "improper" as well as illegal activities.
The fight will take place next week when the Senate debates a resolution providing $4.35 million to the Governmental Affairs Committee to carry out the investigation.

Democrats blame Republicans opposed to campaign finance reform for blocking their attempt to look into what they say is a wide-open loophole in election campaign law that allows unlimited "soft money" donations -- the millions of dollars given to political parties rather than specific races.
The Senate Rules Committee voted on party lines Thursday to approve ground rules for the Senate inquiry hammered out by Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott, capping a lengthy partisan fight.
The issue of "soft money" has come to the fore recently with disclosure that Vice President Al Gore solicited funds for the Democratic Party in phone calls made from the White House.
It has also been disclosed that first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton's chief of staff, Maggie Williams, took a political donation from a California businessman at the White House in 1995.

"What I want ... is a complete unloading about everything there is to know about campaign finance. What this was yesterday was an attempt to limit that kind of investigation," Democratic Sen. John Glenn of Ohio told a news conference.
Sen. Carl Levin, a Michigan Democrat, said the Democrats believed that "we should look both at what is illegal... but we also must look at what is improper ... and should be illegal."

Glenn, Levin and other Dempocrats said they would seek to restore the investigation's previously planned broader scope when the resolution is debated next week but acknowledged that it would be an uphill fight.
"I don't know how people will be able to explain ... why you voted against having a committee of Congress looking at improper ativities," said Sen. Joseph Lieberman, a Connecticut Democrat.

The Republican chairman of the Rules Committee that approved the mandate for the investigation, Sen. John Warner of Virginia, told reporters later: "I think the word illegal gives them sufficient breadth to do the work."
